## Session 184 (2026-07-28) — source-read confirmed candidate (a) is mechanistically real (a strict priority-greater-than scheduler gate can strand a low-priority thread), landed and validated a scheduler-decision instrument to test it; one soak died before reaching the stall region to a distinct, previously-uncatalogued SIGBUS signature inside `evalCubicSplineAtTime`

### Work unit
NEXT.md step 1: source-read the three -35 candidates before instrumenting. Read
`lib/N64ModernRuntime/ultramodern/src/threads.cpp` (`resume_thread_tagged`,
`run_next_thread`, `run_next_thread_and_wait`) and `scheduling.cpp`
(`schedule_running_thread`, `swap_to_thread`, `check_running_queue`,
`pause_self`/`yield_self`) end to end, plus `mesgqueue.cpp`'s `do_send`/`do_recv`
blocking paths.

### Finding: two structurally different "who runs next" mechanisms exist, and only one is priority-blind
- `check_running_queue()` (called after every non-blocking `osSendMesg`/
  `osJamMesg`/`osRecvMesg`, `osSetThreadPri`, `osStartThread`) only swaps to the
  head of `running_queue` if `next_thread->priority > self->priority` —
  **strictly greater**. A tie or a lower-priority queued thread is left
  queued, untouched, and the function returns silently.
- `run_next_thread()` (reached only via `run_next_thread_and_wait`, itself only
  called from `do_send`/`do_recv`'s **blocking** loops in `mesgqueue.cpp` and
  from `osStopThread`'s self-stop path, and from `_thread_func`'s natural-exit
  path) pops `running_queue` **unconditionally**, ignoring priority entirely.
- Consequence: a thread queued into `running_queue` via `schedule_running_thread`
  (the wake-a-blocked-thread path in `do_send`/`do_recv`) is only guaranteed to
  run again if *some* thread, at some point, executes a genuine blocking wait
  (hitting the unconditional pop) — never-preempting priority comparisons alone
  cannot resume it if every thread that subsequently calls
  `check_running_queue` has priority ≥ the queued thread's.
- Checked this against real data already on disk from s183's `schedguard4/`
  run.log (`[thr-create-id]` lines, no new soak needed): `mainBootstrapWorker`
  (thread id=3, entry `0x80000C68` — the hangar-loop/graphics-task-producer
  thread per s93) is created at **priority 10**, one of the lowest of any
  active thread in the roster; `viRetraceHandlerThread` (entry `0x80019868`)
  runs at **priority 117**, and the three audio-related id=0 threads
  (entries `0x8001C328`/`0x80019BF4`/`0x8008ED70`, the last confirmed s70/71
  as `runAiAudioStreamPlaybackLoop`) run at **117-122**. This is exactly the
  priority shape the mechanism needs: if thread 3 is ever queued by a
  non-blocking send/recv from one of these ≥117-priority threads, and none of
  them subsequently performs a genuine blocking wait, thread 3 stays parked
  with **zero** `resume_thread_tagged` activity of any kind — matching s183's
  "0 `thr-resume-skip`, 0 resume activity near the stall" observation exactly,
  and doing so **without needing the s84 UAF guard to fire at all**.

### Instrument landed (`lib/N64ModernRuntime`, pure host C++, no guest/fixup changes)
`ROGUESQ_LOG_SCHED=1` (new env gate, mirrors `ROGUESQ_LOG_THREAD_RESUME`'s
cached-getenv pattern; **not** always-on because both call sites are hot —
`check_running_queue` and `run_next_thread` run on every message send/recv,
same class of hot path s93 found perturbs timing when logged verbosely):
- `scheduling.cpp` `schedule_running_thread`: `[sched-queue] thr=%p id=%d
  pri=%d` — every time a thread is queued into `running_queue`.
- `scheduling.cpp` `check_running_queue`: `[sched-check] self_thr=%p
  self_id=%d self_pri=%d head_thr=%p head_id=%d head_pri=%d swap=%d` — only
  inside the already-existing `!thread_queue_empty()` branch, so it does not
  fire on the common (queue-empty) case.
- `threads.cpp` `run_next_thread`: `[sched-runnext] popped_thr=%p popped_id=%d
  popped_pri=%d` — every unconditional pop.
Patch exported (`./submodule-patches/export.sh` — only
`submodule-patches/N64ModernRuntime.patch` changed, `rt64.patch` untouched)
and committed this session. Built clean via `cmake --build build`
(`DEVELOPER_DIR=/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer`), 0 errors, only
pre-existing SDL2-compat linker version warnings.

### Soak (`schedguard5`, same env block as `schedguard3`/`schedguard4` plus `ROGUESQ_LOG_SCHED=1`)
Positive control fired: 72382 `[sched-queue]`, 333003 `[sched-check]`, 72380
`[sched-runnext]` lines. **Died at hold-iter 6** (`decisionN=8327`), well
*before* the `#9770`-`#9792`-equivalent stall-onset region s180/s183 both
reached (~decision 9770-9792) — this run never got far enough to test the
hypothesis directly. Death: **SIGBUS (signal 10)** inside `evalCubicSplineAtTime
+ 2552`, called from `buildPositionAndCallTransformHelper` →
`setupActorAnchorTransformType1` → `static_5_800AB658` → `static_5_800AAD9C` →
`static_5_800C6854` → `menuOverlayInit` → `mainGameLoop` →
`mainBootstrapWorker`. **This is not the s83-guarded crash** — s83's guard
targets a `NAN_CHECK` assert abort (signal 6/SIGABRT) at one specific
division site (`0x8001906C`); this is a bus error (signal 10, an out-of-bounds
memory access), a different signal and almost certainly a different fault
site within the same function, not previously catalogued under this name.
Not root-caused this session (would need its own source read — flagged, not
chased, per the "don't spend a soak chasing an unrelated crash" posture that
already applies to `rs_free`/`rebuildActiveDisplayObjectList`).

### What the pre-crash data does say (non-discriminating for -35, but not nothing)
In the ~8300 decisions before death, `[sched-queue]` (72382) and
`[sched-runnext]` (72380) counts are within 2 of each other — i.e. in normal
(non-stalled) operation, almost every thread that gets queued does
subsequently get an unconditional-pop chance; starvation via the strict
priority gate is **not** the routine case. This refines rather than confirms
the hypothesis: reaching the stall would require the unconditional-pop path
(`run_next_thread`) to stop firing *for any thread* right around the stall
onset — not a generic, ever-present race. The right discriminating check for
a future run that reaches the stall: does `[sched-runnext]` stop appearing
entirely in the window after the last `[sched-queue]` that names the producer
thread's `thr=` pointer.

### Rules out / keeps

## Session 187 (2026-07-28) — landed the mandatory-pivot defensive guard on `rs_free`'s free-list walk (3 loops, `N64Recomp/fixup_game_funcs.py`), positive control fired 1901x on ONE persistent corrupted node, and the soak survived the ENTIRE 120s hold + grace window with zero crashes — first fully crash-free full-length run anywhere in the s180-187 `schedcaller`/`schedguard`/`rsfreeguard` lineage

### What ran
Per NEXT.md's mandatory pivot (s186 closed the `ROGUESQ_LOG_SCHED` rule-8
budget at 3/3 inconclusive): source-read `rs_free`
(`N64Recomp/RecompiledFuncs/funcs_0.c:3106`, confirmed itself a
`RECOMP_FUNC` — a single shared guest function, so a guard inside it covers
every caller including `rebuildActiveDisplayObjectList` (s183/s186) and
`freeManifestSegmentAssets` (s167/s185) at once). Found `rs_free` contains
**3 near-identical coalescing free-list walk loops**
(`L_80001CE0`/`L_80001DCC`/`L_80001EB4`), each computing
`next = node + size_field` with **zero bounds checking anywhere in the
recomp memory macros** (`N64Recomp/include/recomp.h`'s `MEM_W`/`MEM_HU` do
raw pointer arithmetic into the `rdram` buffer, no clamp) and then
dereferencing through that computed address a few instructions later. s186's
own `[rs-free-walk]` log had already shown the shape: `node=0x80160120
flags=0x0 size=2155119224` — a garbage size that overflows the node's
address 27 MB past the 8 MB RDRAM window (`ram_size = 0x800000`,
`lib/N64ModernRuntime/librecomp/src/sp.cpp:23`), guaranteeing a wild
dereference on the very next access.

Landed a guard (mirroring the s173 `rs_malloc` walk-loop-deref-guard
precedent exactly: same `0x80000000u`/`0x80800000u` RDRAM bounds, same
`goto` to the loop's own natural "terminator bit already set" exit label
instead of continuing to dereference) at all 3 walk loops, gated by a
single new env var `ROGUESQ_LOG_RS_FREE_WALK_GUARD`, logging
`[rs-free-walk-guard] loop=<1|2|3> n=<fire count> bad_next=<addr>
node=<addr> ra=<addr>` on trip. Loop 1's bail target is `L_80001D94`, loop
2's is `L_80001E80`, loop 3's is `L_80001F64` (the function's own
lock-release-and-return tail) — each chosen to exactly match that loop's
existing "list search ends here" control-flow shape, not skip any
additional coalescing work beyond what the real terminator path already
skips.

Regenerated fresh (`N64Recomp` was NOT re-run on an already-patched
`funcs_0.c` — regenerated from the ELF first per the non-idempotency rule,
then `fixup_game_funcs.py` once): fixup log confirms all 3 new patches at
exactly x1 (`funcs_0.c: rs_free free-list walk-loop deref guard loop{1,2,3}
patched x1`), plus the pre-existing s140/s168 rs_free patches also at x1
each (no duplication). Built clean
(`DEVELOPER_DIR=.../Xcode.app/... cmake --build build`).

One soak (`rsfreeguard1`, same env block as `run_schedguard7.sh` plus
`ROGUESQ_LOG_RS_FREE_WALK_GUARD=1`, `ROGUESQ_LOG_SCHED=1` kept armed): the
process **survived the entire 120s hold window + 0s grace and had to be
killed manually** (`game process still alive; killing`) — `CRASH: 0` in the
driver summary. `[rs-free-walk-guard]` fired **1901 times**, all
`loop=1`, all on the exact same node/corruption pair
(`node=0x807982B6 bad_next=0x8475841C`) — a single persistently-corrupted
free-list node that `rs_free` re-encounters on every single call for the
rest of the run, now safely bailed every time instead of crashing on
(what must have been, pre-guard) an eventual unlucky hit. `[sched-queue]`/
`[sched-runnext]`: 131076/131075 — near-balanced, consistent with s184-186.

### Rules out / keeps
- **This specific `rs_free` free-list-walk corruption family (killed s183,
  s185, s186 — 3 of the last 4 scheduling-line attempts) is now defended
  against at its walk site.** Positive control is unambiguous: 1901 fires
  in one run, process did not crash. This is a local guard (buying
  runway), NOT a fix for the underlying corruption that puts the insane
  size value in the free list in the first place — that chase (s85-s114)
  is still open and this session did not touch it.
- **New data point for that still-open corruption chase, not investigated
  further this session**: unlike s173's `rs_malloc` guard (corruption
  proved racy across runs — 0/0 fires with 17,683 clean calls one run),
  this `rs_free` corruption looks **deterministic within a run once it
  occurs** — the same node/bad_next pair fired on essentially every `rs_free`
  call for the remainder of the soak (1901x), not a rare one-off. Worth
  keeping in mind if/when the corruption-source chase resumes: this
  particular node persists in the free list rather than being cleaned up
  or re-corrupted differently each time.
- **Did not observe or rule out the `-35` stall itself this run.** The
  crash-only `[CRASH][vifs-snapshot] decisionN=...` counter is the only
  place `ROGUESQ_LOG_SCHED`'s decision number gets printed — with no
  crash this run, there is no decision-number readout at all, so we cannot
  tell whether this run passed through, sustained, or never reached the
  historical stall window. `[sched-queue]`/`[sched-runnext]` staying
  near-balanced for the whole run is at least consistent with "never
  stalled," matching s183/s186's balanced-until-the-crash pattern, but is
  not itself proof either way. **Instrumentation gap for next session**:
  a periodic (not just crash-time) `decisionN` log line would let a
  crash-free run like this one actually report whether it stalled.

### Carried-forward open items

1. **Add a periodic (non-crash-gated) `[sched-decision]`-style log tick**
   (e.g. every N decisions, or on a wall-clock timer) so a crash-free run
   can report whether/when it hit the `-35` stall, since this session's

   candidate (a) (`ROGUESQ_LOG_SCHED`'s own hypothesis, rule-8 budget

lineage's own narrative.

guard"**: this is NOT a fresh, unguarded crash site — `N64Recomp/

(`..._LIST_GUARD2`/`..._LIST_GUARD3`, s99-101-era), and s175's
recursion-depth cap (`ROGUESQ_LOG_SCENE_NODE_DEPTH_GUARD`, static counter,

## Session 190 (2026-07-28) — corrected a documentation error in s189's "4 existing guards on processSceneNode" claim (only 1 of the 4 actually touches that function), landed the missing node-pointer guard, caught and fixed a self-introduced regression via a control-run comparison, then hit a different, already-catalogued crash before reaching the target decision window

**Correction before doing anything else**: NEXT.md/CURRENT-TRUTH item -38 said
`N64Recomp/fixup_game_funcs.py` carries "4 guards on this exact function
(`processSceneNode`)" and that none of them fired in `schedtick1`. Cross-
referencing guest addresses (not just guard names) against the function
boundaries (`grep -n "^RECOMP_FUNC" funcs_4.c`) shows this was wrong: 3 of the
4 (`_scene_node_list_guard_patch`/`_guard2`/`_guard3`, fixup script lines
~2337-2478) are patched into **`submitSceneNodeRender`** (funcs_4.c:6-2999,
guest ~0x8000FEA0-0x800112xx) — a completely different function that guards
its own free-list allocator walk and is not even in this crash's call stack.
Only s175's recursion-depth cap (fixup script lines ~3899-3990) actually
touches `processSceneNode` (funcs_4.c:13759-14879), and it only counts calls —
it never validates the node pointer itself. So the interior of
`processSceneNode` had **zero** real deref guards, not 3, before this session.
This doesn't overturn s189's core finding (the crash is one specific unguarded
dereference, not a depth phenomenon) but it does mean the "none of 4 guards
fired" evidence was 4x weaker than it looked — only 1 of the citations was
actually a relevant null result.

**Source-read** (`processSceneNode`/`traverseSceneGraphRecursive`,
funcs_4.c:13759-15184, building on s175's own groundwork comment) found the
mechanism NEXT.md asked for: `traverseSceneGraphRecursive` walks a sibling
list rooted at mutable global `0x80112B20`, reading each node's own "next"
field at offset 0 with zero bounds checking (funcs_4.c:15073-15074,
`ctx->r3 = MEM_W(ctx->r3, 0X0)`), then passes that same raw pointer straight
into the recursive `processSceneNode(rdram, ctx)` call as its `a2` argument
— which becomes `processSceneNode`'s own node pointer (`ctx->r17`/$s1,
funcs_4.c:13766-13767) and is dereferenced immediately on entry
(funcs_4.c:13792 pre-patch, `MEM_W(ctx->r17, 0XC)`) with no validation
anywhere in between. A single corrupted "next" field anywhere in the sibling
chain flows straight through the recursive-call boundary into a raw
dereference — explaining the fixed native-offset SIGBUS across independent
recurrences/rebuilds without needing a depth-overflow explanation.

**Fix landed**: a new entry-point guard on `processSceneNode`'s node pointer
(`ctx->r17`), checked once right after s175's depth cap and before the first
dereference, bailing to the same `L_80015528` exit with the same `ctx->r2=0`
sentinel the caller's sibling-loop condition already reads as "stop
iterating this level" (`N64Recomp/fixup_game_funcs.py`, new
`ROGUESQ_LOG_SCENE_NODE_PTR_GUARD` env var, `[scene-node-ptr-guard]` log
tag). Full regen (`make_elf.py` not needed, only fixup script changed →
`regen_n64recomp.sh` → `fixup_game_funcs.py` once, confirmed `x1` for the new
patch and all 3 pre-existing `processSceneNode`-adjacent patches still `x1`,
no duplication) → `cmake --build`, exit 0, only pre-existing-class warnings.

**Caught and fixed a self-introduced regression before it could contaminate
the result** (this is itself the most reusable finding this session): the
first version of the patch's regex match consumed the pre-existing
`ctx->r3 = MEM_W(ctx->r17, 0XC);` line as a stable anchor but the replacement
function never re-emitted it, silently **deleting that instruction** from
the compiled function. Two soaks on that build (`sceneptrguard1`,
`sceneptrguard2`, same env block as s188's `schedtick1` plus the new guard's
env var) both crashed **immediately and byte-identically** at
decisionN=151/149 — a brand-new signature never seen before
(`submitSceneNodeRender+2156` self-call, called from `processSceneNode`,
never a scene the game had reached this early in any prior soak) — with the
new guard's own log tag **never firing** (0/0), which was the tell: the
guard's mere presence, not its activation, was changing behavior, pointing
at a codegen bug rather than a triggered false-positive. Built and ran a
control (`controlnoguard1`): identical env block, only the new patch
disabled (temporarily neutered via `if False and p.name == ...`) — survived
the **entire 120s hold + grace window with zero crashes**, decisionN reached
14721+ before being killed manually. That confirmed the regression was
caused by the patch itself, not the pre-existing lib state, and pointed
straight at the deleted deref line once the diff was re-examined. Fixed by
re-appending the original line to the replacement string; regenerated,
confirmed `x1` again, rebuilt.

**Post-fix soak (`sceneptrguard3`)**: no regression — decisionN climbed
cleanly through a real VI-width transition (1024→512, a legitimate mission
load, not a crash) to **8053** before dying to a SIGBUS in
`reserveAndEmitDLEntry` (called via `submitSceneNodeRender` ←
`processSceneNode` ← `traverseSceneGraphRecursive` (twice, +1576/+2336) ←
`setupCameraMatrices` ← ...). This is the **already-catalogued 14th class**
(`reserveAndEmitDLEntry`, first identified s168-171, PORTING-STATE ~15574-
15780) recurring at a native offset (+5212) past both the s109 guard and the
3 guards s169 added — a whack-a-mole-shaped "another unguarded deref in the
same function" recurrence, not a new bug family. **`scene-node-ptr-guard`
did not fire** (0) — meaning this run never reached a call where the node
pointer was actually corrupted, so **the guard's effectiveness against the
target processSceneNode self-recursion bug (9660-9800 decisionN window) is
still untested** — the run was blocked by a different, earlier crash before
it could get there.

### Result

1. Corrected CURRENT-TRUTH item -38: only 1 of the "4 existing guards" is
   actually on `processSceneNode`; the other 3 guard an unrelated function
   (`submitSceneNodeRender`).
2. Landed `ROGUESQ_LOG_SCENE_NODE_PTR_GUARD` on `processSceneNode`'s node
   pointer (`N64Recomp/fixup_game_funcs.py`, funcs_4.c entry, mirrors the
   depth-cap's bail semantics).
3. Found, root-caused, and fixed a self-introduced regression (deleted
   instruction from an over-greedy regex match) using a same-session control
   build as the discriminating test — 2/2 crash with the bug, 1/1 crash-free
   past decisionN 14721+ with the same patch disabled.
4. The actual target question (does the fixed guard let decisionN push past
   9792, and does the `-35` stall signature appear) is **still open** — this
   run hit a different, already-catalogued crash (`reserveAndEmitDLEntry`,
   14th class) at decisionN=8053 first. Not evidence against the fix; just
   an earlier obstacle in the same run.

No `submodule-patches/export.sh` needed — all edits this session were in the
standalone `N64Recomp` tool checkout (`fixup_game_funcs.py`,
`RecompiledFuncs/*.c` regenerated output) and `RogueSquadron64Recomp/scratch/
agent/*`, nothing under `RogueSquadron64Recomp/lib/`.

## Session 193 (2026-07-28) — attempted Option A (guard the `runVideoFrameTick` crash), found the crash site can't be safely guarded without disassembly tooling this session has none of; pivoted to Option B and CLOSED it — the s192 `queueGPUUploadTMEM` guard now has a confirmed-live positive control

**Option A attempt, and why it was abandoned (not a wasted step — a real
negative result):** NEXT.md's Option A asked to read the full body of
`runVideoFrameTick` (`N64Recomp/RecompiledFuncs/funcs_0.c:1459`, ~415 lines)
and find the actual faulting dereference at native offset `+1568`
(`0x00000001040b7cb8`, confirmed via `sceneptrguard5/run.log:3958648-49` —
the address that killed s192's soak). The recompiled-C source at that MIPS
instruction range doesn't map 1:1 to the compiled ARM64 binary's byte
offsets, so the only way to identify the actual faulting instruction is to
disassemble the binary at that offset — and `nm`/`otool`/`lldb`/`objdump`
are not on this session's Bash allowlist (confirmed: `otool` triggers an
approval prompt a non-interactive session can't clear). Wrote a
from-scratch Mach-O symbol-table reader + minimal ARM64 load/store decoder
(`scratch/agent/machoparse.py` already existed for symbol addr/size;
added `scratch/agent/s193_disasm.py` for the actual instruction decode,
`scratch/agent/s193_symrange.py` to rule out a hidden local-symbol
boundary). Result: confirmed no other symbol (local or external) exists
between `runVideoFrameTick` and `coalesceFreeHeapBlocks`, so offset+1568 is
unambiguously inside `runVideoFrameTick`'s own compiled body — but the
decoded instruction at that exact offset is `0x14000001`, an unconditional
branch (`B pc+4`), which cannot itself raise a bus error, and the
instruction immediately before it hand-decodes as a `BL` with an
implausibly large (~19 MB) target offset for a ~5 KB function, which reads
as a decode error somewhere in my by-hand bit-field arithmetic rather than
real code. **Conclusion: a hand-rolled ARM64 decoder without cross-checking
against a real disassembler is not trustworthy enough to place a guard
on** — NEXT.md explicitly warned "do not guess a guard site from the
backtrace alone," and guessing off a self-decoded instruction stream with a
demonstrated internal inconsistency is exactly that. Did not add a guard.
This crash stays uncatalogued/unguarded; a future session should either
get a real disassembler approved onto the Bash allowlist (`otool -tv` or
`objdump -d --start-address=... --stop-address=...` on `build/
RogueSquadron64Recomp`) or extend the hand-rolled decoder far enough to be
self-consistent before trusting it again.

## Session 194 (2026-07-28) — disassembly tools still blocked (confirmed again); pivoted to a source-level fix instead — the SIGSEGV/SIGBUS handler now dumps siginfo + the full ARM64 register file, and its FIRST soak both reached a new furthest decisionN (9741, inside the 9660-9792 target window) and caught a brand-new, precisely-characterized crash via the register dump alone, with no disassembler at all

**Disassembly tooling: confirmed still blocked, did not re-litigate.**
Retried NEXT.md's Option A first-step exactly as specified: plain
`otool -tv -p` and `objdump --disassemble-symbols=` against
`build/RogueSquadron64Recomp`, as ordinary non-piped Bash calls. Both
required approval and were denied in this non-interactive session, same as
s193. Per NEXT.md's own guidance ("try once at the start... if still
blocked, don't burn budget re-attempting"), did not retry a 3rd time and
did not touch `s193_disasm.py` (still unvalidated, still not trusted).

**Pivot: the crash handler was silently discarding its own best evidence.**
Reading the existing POSIX signal handler
(`src/main/main.cpp:1654-1683`) to plan the decoder-validation sub-step
turned up a cheaper, more reliable path: it installs with `SA_SIGINFO`
(`sa.sa_flags = SA_SIGINFO | SA_RESETHAND`) but the handler lambda was
`[](int sig, siginfo_t*, void*)` — both the `siginfo_t*` (has `si_addr`,
the exact faulting virtual address) and the `void*` `ucontext_t*` (has the
full ARM64 register file: `x0`-`x28`, `fp`, `lr`, `sp`, `pc`, `cpsr`, plus
`__es.__far`/`__esr`/`__exception`, all inside `uc_mcontext->__ss`/`__es`
on Darwin/arm64) were being discarded. This is strictly better than
disassembly for identifying a bad-pointer crash: instead of inferring which
register held the bad value from the instruction encoding, the register
file at the exact fault instant is just... there, already captured by the
kernel, for free. No new build risk beyond the crash path itself (all other
code paths unaffected).

**Change:** `src/main/main.cpp` — added `#include <sys/ucontext.h>` (not
`<ucontext.h>`, which requires `_XOPEN_SOURCE` on this SDK and errored:
"deprecated ucontext routines require _XOPEN_SOURCE to be defined"; the
BSD-style `<sys/ucontext.h>` header exposes the same `ucontext_t`/
`mcontext_t` struct layout without that guard). Extended the lambda to
print `[CRASH][siginfo] si_addr=... si_code=... si_errno=...` and, on
`__APPLE__ && __aarch64__`, `[CRASH][mcontext] pc=... far=... esr=...
exception=...` followed by all 29 `x` registers and `fp`/`lr`/`sp`/`cpsr`.
Pure `src/main/main.cpp` change (this repo, not `lib/`) — built with a
plain `cmake --build build --target RogueSquadron64Recomp -j`, no
regen/fixup pipeline needed, builds clean (2 pre-existing unrelated
deprecation warnings in `rt64`'s vendored `json.hpp`, nothing new).

**Soak (`scratch/agent/run_mcontext1.sh`, tag `mcontext1`, identical env
block to s192/s193's `sceneptrguard5`): the new dump fired, gave a sane,
internally-consistent read, and the run reached the furthest decisionN of
any soak to date.** `CRASH: 34` in the summary (many are the routine
already-catalogued small crashes this soak script's env block doesn't
guard against; the interesting one is the fatal one that ended the run):

```
[CRASH] caught signal 10 (Bus error: 10), dumping stack:
[CRASH][siginfo] si_addr=0x380630062 si_code=1 si_errno=0
[CRASH][mcontext] pc=0x1028cc4a4 far=0x380630062 esr=0x92000006 exception=0x0
[CRASH][mcontext] x0 =0x0000000300000000   (== x8; almost certainly the rdram host base pointer)
[CRASH][mcontext] x8 =0x0000000300000000
[CRASH][mcontext] x9 =0x0000000080630062   (raw, UNSIGN-EXTENDED KSEG0 guest pointer)
... (x1-x7, x10-x28 mostly small/zero, not implicated)
[CRASH][mcontext] fp=0x000000016fe628c0 lr=0x00000001028ee4fc sp=0x000000016fe62890 cpsr=0xa0000000
[CRASH][vifs-snapshot] decisionN=9741 lastFireDecisionN=9740 decisionsSinceFire=1 lastFireWasStalled=0 stalledNow=0
3   RogueSquadron64Recomp   0x00000001028ee4fc processSceneNode + 8772
5   RogueSquadron64Recomp   0x00000001028ef910 traverseSceneGraphRecursive + 1576
```
(`scratch/s73_post_a_scene/mcontext1/run.log:4468133-4468166`)

**Reading the register file directly identifies the bug class, no
disassembly needed:** `far` (== `si_addr`, self-consistent) decomposes
exactly as `x0/x8 (0x300000000) + x9 (0x80630062)` — the host rdram base
pointer plus a guest pointer that STILL HAS its KSEG0 tag (`0x80000000`)
intact and is zero-extended (upper 32 bits of x9 are 0), not sign-extended.
Compare `N64Recomp/include/recomp.h`'s `MEM_W` macro (the normal/correct
path): `rdram + ((reg + offset) - 0xFFFFFFFF80000000)`, which only works
because `ADD32` sign-extends 32-bit register values through `(gpr)(int32_t)(...)`
to `0xFFFFFFFF80xxxxxx` before the macro subtracts the KSEG0 base. Here,
whatever computed this address added the RAW, zero-extended 32-bit guest
value directly to the rdram base with NO KSEG0 subtraction at all — a
different, less-safe code path than `MEM_W`, producing an ~2 GB wild
pointer instead of a valid ~8 MB rdram offset. This is a genuinely new
mechanism, distinct from every previously-catalogued crash in this
project's history (none of which were characterized as a masking/sign-
extension bug before). `lr=processSceneNode+8772` is the RETURN address of
a call from inside `processSceneNode` (`N64Recomp/RecompiledFuncs/funcs_4.c:13759-14873`)
to whatever's at the actual faulting `pc` — the unwinder couldn't resolve a
symbol for `pc` itself (likely a small/leaf helper with no separate frame),
which is why the backtrace shows the caller. **Single-source, first
occurrence** — `grep -l "processSceneNode + 8772" scratch/s73_post_a_scene/*/run.log`
matches only this run; not yet confirmed as a recurring crash class the
way `queueGPUUploadTMEM`/`rs_malloc` are.

**Milestone: furthest decisionN yet, and it's INSIDE the target window.**
Prior furthest was s192's 8972; this soak reached 9741, past the
`[scene-node-ptr-guard]` target window's start (9660) and still short of
its end (9792). `[scene-node-ptr-guard]` fired 0 times again (now 0/4
across all soaks) — this NEW crash killed the run before the guarded site
could be exercised, so the s190 fix is STILL untested, but the accumulated
guards from s190-s193 are demonstrably doing their job: this is the first
soak to ever get this deep. Did not attempt to pinpoint the exact source
statement or add a guard this session — that's real, separate, bounded
work (need to identify which call site inside `processSceneNode` passes an
unmasked pointer, most likely by finding a place that skips `MEM_W`/`ADD32`
and does raw pointer arithmetic) and this session's actual deliverable
(the mcontext instrument) is already a complete, validated, standalone
unit. Two runs is not enough to know if this crash is itself the new
soak-blocking bottleneck or a one-off; that's the natural next probe.

**What this does and doesn't show:**
- DOES confirm the new `[CRASH][siginfo]`/`[CRASH][mcontext]` dump is live,
  reachable, and produces internally-consistent, sane values (positive
  control: `si_addr == far`, `x0 == x8`, the decomposition arithmetic checks
  out exactly) — this is now a permanent, always-on diagnostic (no env
  gate needed; it's pure stderr text on an already-fatal path, costs
  nothing on the non-crash path).
- DOES identify a real, previously-invisible bug MECHANISM (KSEG0-tagged
  pointer added to rdram base without the usual sign-extend + subtract) —
  but from ONE occurrence. Treat as a strong lead, not a confirmed
  root-cause, until it recurs or is traced to a specific source line.
- DOES NOT touch or replace any existing guard (`scene-node-ptr`,
  `tmem-zero`, depth-cap, etc.) — all read-only diagnostic, added purely
  inside the crash-signal path.
- DOES NOT resolve the `runVideoFrameTick` crash from s192/s193 — it simply
  didn't recur this run (this soak died to a different, new crash before
  reaching that code path, or reached a state where it no longer applies;
  not investigated further this session).
- Confirms the project's crash handler had a several-session-old blind
  spot: `SA_SIGINFO` was being requested but its payload thrown away. Any
  future SIGSEGV/SIGBUS in this project now gets this register dump for
  free, no rebuild required.

## Session 199 (2026-07-28) — added a source-level defensive guard on `runVideoFrameTick`'s 3 global video-state-pointer derefs (disassembly still blocked); 2 informative soaks show no recurrence of the `+1568` crash, but a 3rd soak's DEATH is itself the headline: a byte-for-byte 2nd occurrence of s194's single-occurrence `processSceneNode+8772` KSEG0-zero-extension bug, promoting it to the new top-priority confirmed-recurring crash

### Disassembly tooling: re-confirmed still blocked, did not retry further

Per NEXT.md step 1, tried `otool -tv build/RogueSquadron64Recomp` fresh this
session as a plain non-piped Bash call. Result: `"This command requires
approval"` — no human is present in this non-interactive session to clear
it, same outcome s193/s194 already established. Did not retry a 2nd time
(NEXT.md's own guidance) and did not touch the hand-rolled decoder
(`s193_disasm.py`, already shown untrustworthy). Went straight to step 2,
the broad defensive-guard fallback.

### What ran — the guard

A full read of `runVideoFrameTick` (`N64Recomp/RecompiledFuncs/funcs_0.c:1459`,
the whole ~415-line/177-MIPS-instruction function, confirmed still exactly
this range) found the function's derefs fall into two clearly distinct
classes: the vast majority use pointers that come directly from the
function's own arguments (`$s3`/`$s0`/`$s2`, `ctx->r19`/`r16`/`r18`) —
exercised on literally every call across every soak this project has ever
run, with zero attributable crashes. But at 3 sites (MIPS
`0x8000154C`/`0x8000157C`/`0x800015BC`) the function instead LOADS A POINTER
FROM A FIXED GLOBAL RDRAM ADDRESS (`lui $v0,0x8011; lw $v0,-0x350($v0)` ==
guest `0x8010FCB0`) and immediately dereferences it via raw `MEM_W`/
`do_swl`/`do_swr` writes (offsets `0x10`-`0x44`) with zero validation — the
same "cached/global pointer, never checked" shape as every previously
guarded crash class in this project (s99, s100, s109, s169, s197's
`scene-node-cache-guard`). All 3 writes are gated behind a chain of
conditional branches upstream (`reapplyDisplayMode` returning 0, a byte flag
at `$s2+4`, etc.), so this global is exercised far less often than the rest
of the function — consistent with an intermittent, thousands-of-decisions-deep
crash rather than an every-call one.

Cross-checked against s198's own crash evidence: the s194 crash-handler
upgrade recorded `si_addr=0x320000000` for this exact `+1568` crash — many
GB past any valid rdram offset, the signature of an unmasked/garbage
pointer, not a near-miss. This matches the global-pointer hypothesis:
`MEM_W` (`N64Recomp/include/recomp.h`) is completely unbounded (
`rdram + ((reg+offset) - 0xFFFFFFFF80000000)`, no range check at all,
relies entirely on the register holding a correctly sign-extended
`0x80000000`-`0x807FFFFF` guest address) — if the global at `0x8010FCB0` is
ever 0/uninitialized/corrupt, the resulting host pointer lands wildly
outside the 8 MB rdram buffer.

Guarded all 3 sites (`N64Recomp/fixup_game_funcs.py`, `funcs_0.c`,
`ROGUESQ_LOG_VIDEO_FRAME_TICK_GUARD`): after each load, check the pointer is
in the valid RDRAM range; if not, log (env-gated) and skip ONLY that site's
reads+writes (confirmed by reading the surrounding code that every register
touched is freshly reloaded by the next site or the function epilogue — no
stale-value hazard from skipping). Unlike s197's cache guard, does NOT reset
the global to a known-safe value — its true semantics (likely a camera/
video-mode state struct, not a free-list head) aren't established, so
overwriting it could introduce a new bug; skip-only is the minimal,
defensible change. Full regen (`make_elf.py` → `N64Recomp` →
`fixup_game_funcs.py` → `cmake --build`) ran clean; verified the patch
applied exactly once per site (`grep -c "video-frame-tick-guard"
funcs_0.c` → 3, not 6). Pure `N64Recomp/fixup_game_funcs.py` change (outside
this repo, flagged for the user per standing convention, not committed by
this session).

## Session 207 (2026-07-28) — targeted re-read of `renderUnlitMeshFaces` at the `+508` offset: still clean, but a build-config check settles the standing "could the callee be inlined" question and revises the offset->source-line mapping confidence

**Goal**: NEXT.md's prescribed work unit — re-read `renderUnlitMeshFaces`
(`N64Recomp/RecompiledFuncs/funcs_4.c:4951-5605`) with the `+508`-byte dladdr
offset (s206) as a targeted map, not a blind whole-function pass, to find the
`+8772` KSEG0-zero-extension bug's root cause inside the one function s206's
new pc-symbol diagnostic named directly.

**Step 1 — re-verify disassembly tools are still blocked (2 independent
attempts, not just precedent)**: `nm ./RogueSquadron64Recomp` (from `build/`)
and `atos -o build/RogueSquadron64Recomp -l 0x104564000 0x104c24a60` (using
s206's own captured pc/base pair, which would have given a direct
source-file:line resolution if it worked, entirely sidestepping the
byte-offset-guessing exercise below) — **both denied**, "This command requires
approval," in this non-interactive session. Confirms s202-206's note is still
current; not re-litigating this again barring an environment change.

**Step 2 — a build-config fact that answers a standing open question**: grepped
`CMakeLists.txt` for the RecompiledFuncs target and found (line 239, s38's own
comment): **this whole project builds `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` (`-O0`), and
`RecompiledFuncs` (which holds `funcs_4.c`/`funcs_6.c`) is NOT in the
short-list of 3 translation units (`FACTOR5_UCODE_C`/`_B_C`/`_BOOT_C`) that get
an explicit `-O2` override.** So `renderUnlitMeshFaces` and its callee both
compile fully unoptimized. Separately, `RECOMP_FUNC` (`N64Recomp/include/recomp.h:22`)
expands to `extern inline __attribute__((weak,noinline))` on the clang/GCC
branch this build uses — **every recompiled game function, including
`getTextureLUTFieldAt8`, is explicitly `noinline`.**

Together these two facts **definitively rule out** the possibility raised
while re-reading this session (see Step 3): that `renderUnlitMeshFaces+508`
in the crash log could actually be *inside* an inlined call to
`getTextureLUTFieldAt8` (the function's one and only callee — grepped the
full `4951-5605` range for the `[A-Za-z_]+\(rdram, *ctx\);` call pattern s206
used on `processSceneNode`, exactly one hit). `noinline` + `-O0` means that
call is a real, separate machine-code jump to a real, separate symbol; a
fault inside it would dladdr-resolve to `getTextureLUTFieldAt8+N`, not
`renderUnlitMeshFaces+508`. **The crash is confirmed to be genuinely inside
`renderUnlitMeshFaces`'s own body**, closing off a branch that would otherwise
have needed its own investigation.

`-O0` also revises (upward in confidence, but not to certainty) the
offset-to-source-line linear-mapping assumption NEXT.md flagged as unverified:
no inlining, no cold-path splitting, no instruction scheduling/reordering at
`-O0` — source order should track machine-code order much more faithfully
than under `-O2`. The magnitude of the ARM64-instructions-per-MIPS-line ratio
is still unmeasured (no calibration point exists — this is the only
`[CRASH][pc-symbol]` line captured so far, see PORTING-STATE grep), and `-O0`
tends to be *more* verbose per statement (stack-spill-heavy), which could push
the true offset earlier than a naive per-line estimate, not later — so this
is a *directional* refinement, not a solved calibration.

**Step 3 — the actual re-read.** Read `funcs_4.c:4951` through `5605` (the
full function, but line-by-line with the offset framing and the callee
question in mind, not a repeat of s204's method) plus `funcs_6.c:13392-13417`
(the one callee, `getTextureLUTFieldAt8`). Findings:

- The conservative NEXT.md window (`4951-5030`, prologue + the linked-list
  null-check preamble) is unchanged-clean: stack saves, one `ADD32`-derived
  pointer (`s4`/`r20` from the incoming arg), straightforward `MEM_W` reads
  assigned directly into `gpr` (`ctx->rN`) fields, which sign-extend
  correctly via C's implicit `int32_t -> uint64_t` promotion rule on
  assignment (same convention verified for the other five callees since
  s200).
- The one callee call site (`getTextureLUTFieldAt8`, line 5083, ~132 source
  lines / an estimated ballpark of the 127-ARM64-instruction mark) — the
  callee itself (`funcs_6.c:13392-13417`, 11 real instructions) is a clean
  bounded LUT lookup: its one argument is masked `& 0xFFFF` on entry, all
  address math goes through `ADD32`, the one load is `MEM_HU` at a fixed
  `+8` offset whose result is returned directly (a 16-bit field value, not
  used as a pointer). No zero-extension-bypass pattern; also now confirmed
  architecturally non-inlined (Step 2), so this call cannot be the
  `+508`-attributed fault regardless.
- Extended the read past both offset estimates through the rest of the
  function (`5090-5605`) with the same checklist — including the two loop
  back-edges that walk linked-list "next" pointers via `MEM_W(reg, 0)`/`MEM_W(reg,
  4)` (lines 5546, 5563 — exactly the free-list/linked-list pointer-chase
  pattern that has been the root cause of several OTHER guards elsewhere in
  this codebase, e.g. s123/s131's `SCENE_NODE_LIST_GUARD` family, s133's
  `EMIT_DL_GUARD2`/`GUARD3` — so this was checked with extra scrutiny). Both
  reload directly into `ctx->r16`/`ctx->r18` (`gpr`), same correct-sign-extension
  convention. The register restore epilogue (`5586-5599`) is plain stack

  pass — the contradiction s206 raised (dynamic pc evidence vs. static clean
  read) is NOT resolved by finding a source-level bug; the function still
  reads as correct C given every register's provenance traced this session.

**What this rules out**: the `getTextureLUTFieldAt8`-inlining hypothesis
(architecturally impossible per Step 2); a source-level zero-extension bypass
anywhere in `renderUnlitMeshFaces`'s own body (re-confirmed, now twice,
single-source/static-only both times).

**What this does NOT resolve**: why a function that reads clean at the C

(clang `-O0` miscompile) — exotic, unconsidered until now, should stay lowest
priority per the boring-first-explanations rule until (a) and a proper

(`N64Recomp` checkout, not `lib/`) following the codebase's established
`static int s_..._enabled = -1` + `getenv()`-gated GUARD convention, but
deliberately NON-mutating (no `goto`/bail — a pure observer, since altering
control flow here would invalidate reproduction of the very crash being
chased). Added a helper `_rogue_unlit_mesh_tracer_check(site, reg, offset)`
that computes `(reg + offset) - 0xFFFFFFFF80000000` (MEM_W's own formula,
`recomp.h:95-96`) and logs ONLY when the result falls outside `[0, 0x800000)`
(RDRAM's real 8 MiB extent, matching `src/main/main.cpp`'s own convention —
NOT the older GUARDs' `U32(reg)` MIPS-address-range convention, which
truncates to 32 bits and would silently pass a zero-extended register whose
lower 32 bits happen to look like a valid MIPS address; the two failure
detectors are NOT equivalent for this bug class). Also added an unconditional
positive-control call counter (iron rule #1) — logs at call #1 and every
10000th call after, gated behind the same new `ROGUESQ_LOG_UNLIT_MESH_TRACER`
env var. `fixup_game_funcs.py` patch report showed all 4 sites + the helper
patched exactly `x1`, no duplicates. Full regen (`make_elf.py` → `N64Recomp`
→ `fixup_game_funcs.py`) and `cmake --build`, clean, exit 0.

reaching VI width 1024 — crashed in `waitForAnyAudioSlot` (the pre-catalogued,
unrelated 23rd crash class NEXT.md already says not to chase), 0 tracer

crashes**, positive-control counter never logged (0 tracer lines total) —
this was ambiguous, NOT a clean negative: the counter only logs at call #1
or multiples of 10000, and a scene with few visible unlit meshes could
plausibly call the function fewer than 10000 times in 300s without ever
proving it ran. **This is a real gap the design should have caught up front**
— fixed immediately (calls==1 now always logs) rather than accepted as an
inconclusive null result, per the "a null result is worthless without a
positive control" rule. Cheap fix: edited `fixup_game_funcs.py`, deleted only

rebuilt clean.

Positive control fired at call #1 (proves the instrument executed on the
very call that later crashed). **Zero OOB fired at any of the 4 traced
sites.** The process then SIGBUS'd (signal 10) with `si_addr=far=0x380630062`,

call's return point) ← processSceneNode+10408 ← traverseSceneGraphRecursive
← setupCameraMatrices`). Register dump: `x8=0x0000000300000000` (rdram host
base), `x9=0x0000000080630062` (the zero-extended, NOT sign-extended, KSEG0
guest pointer — upper 32 bits are `0x00000000`, should be `0xFFFFFFFF`).

**The cross-reference that makes this session's result matter more than one
more data point**: `far=0x380630062` is not merely "a KSEG0-shaped crash" —
it is the EXACT SAME 64-bit value as s194's original `mcontext1` occurrence.
Grepped `si_addr=0x380630062\|far=0x380630062` across every soak log in
`scratch/s73_post_a_scene/*/run.log` and found it FOUR times: `mcontext1`
(s194, first documented), `videoframetickguard3` (an earlier, undocumented-at-
the-time occurrence, no pc-symbol available then), `pcsymbolize1` (s206,
resolved to `renderUnlitMeshFaces+508`), and this session's `unlitmeshtracer3`
(resolved to `renderUnlitMeshFaces+792`). **This recurring bug is not random
heap/pointer garbage** — the identical byte value `0x80630062` reappearing
across independent runs, independent inputs (different stick-schedule timings
across sessions), and now two DIFFERENT instruction offsets within the same
function, is far more consistent with a specific, deterministic data source
(a fixed asset field, a specific global, or a specific struct offset that
always holds this address) than with heap corruption or a timing race. s194's
"not yet confirmed recurring" is SUPERSEDED — this is confirmed recurring,
4 occurrences, single value.

**What this rules out**: explanation (a) in its NAIVE form — "the SOURCE
register at one of the 4 highest-probability sites is already a bad address
before the dereference" — for whichever of the 4 sites executed before the
crash point this run. Given `lr=+640` sits at the `getTextureLUTFieldAt8`
call's return (source-confirmed at `funcs_4.c:5104`, well after site B's load
at line 5029), site A and site B's checks both necessarily ran and reported
IN_BOUNDS before the crash — i.e., `ctx->r20` (site A/B's source register)
was a valid pointer, and the BYTE READ from `ctx->r20+0x20` (which becomes
`ctx->r16`, site B's result) was itself readable/in-bounds at the time of
that specific load.

**What this does NOT resolve, and sharpens instead of closes**: `ctx->r16`
(loaded at site B) is dereferenced roughly 35 more times between line 5029
and the loop-back reload at 5546 (grepped: lines 5057, 5069, 5114, 5117,
5129, 5141, 5157, 5167, 5177, 5187, 5189, 5191, 5195, 5347-5542) — my 4 sites
only checked the LOAD's source address, never the LOADED VALUE (`ctx->r16`
itself) before its first subsequent use as a base pointer. Per C's implicit
`int32_t -> uint64_t` promotion (verified correct architecturally many times
over s200-207), assigning `ctx->r16 = MEM_W(...)` should ALWAYS sign-extend a
raw 32-bit RDRAM value like `0x80630062` into the correct KSEG0 form
`0xFFFFFFFF80630062` — meaning if `ctx->r16` really held the naive
zero-extended `0x0000000080630062` at the time of the crash, that value did
NOT arrive via the normal `MEM_W`-assignment path this codebase already
audited clean. Two live sub-hypotheses now, neither yet distinguished: (a1)
some OTHER register (not `ctx->r16`) is the actual zero-extended one at the
fault site (ARM64 register `x9` in this dump does not have a confirmed
`ctx->rN` mapping without disassembly, which stays blocked); (a2) the
recurring EXACT value `0x80630062` points at a specific fixed data source
(worth grepping decomp symbol tables / asset headers for this literal
address) rather than a generic "corrupted linked-list node."

**Next work unit** (see rewritten NEXT.md): two candidate probes, pick

earlier than s210's crash (6s into hold) or s211's stall (near the run's
natural 300s end). `unlit-mesh-tracer`/`B_LOADED`: 0 lines again — the
original s208 `ctx->r16` question is STILL unanswered, now 0/5 soaks across
4 sessions (s209/s210/s211/s213) and 3 different varied recipes.

**Crash detail** (`scratch/s73_post_a_scene/unlitmeshtracer8/run.log:141317-
141353`): signal 10 (Bus error), `si_addr=far=0x380003827`,
`decisionN=7988 lastFireDecisionN=7969 decisionsSinceFire=19 stalledNow=0`
(not stall-related — genuine crash during active operation). Register dump:
`x10=0x0000000080003827`, `x11=x12=x13=0x0000000080000000`, all other
general-purpose registers either small stack/heap pointers or zero.

**Finding 1 — live confirmation of the s157/s172 inlining theory.**
`[CRASH][pc-symbol]` (dladdr-based, trusted per NEXT.md environment notes)
names `heapWalker+1128`. `backtrace_symbols_fd`'s own stack dump names the
*same* frame `frameStartReset+532` (duplicated at frames 3 and 4). s157/s172
theorized from a source read alone (never proven with a live crash) that
`frameStartReset`-attributed crashes are actually inside its first,
unconditional callee `heapWalker`, misattributed by imprecise
symbolication — this crash is the first LIVE data point where both
symbolication paths disagree on the exact same frame and the more precise
one (dladdr) names heapWalker. Confirms the theory; not itself new
evidence about heapWalker's specific fault mechanism.

**Finding 2 — the crash's register shape exposes a project-wide guard
design gap, source-confirmed via `recomp.h`.** heapWalker already carries
10 guard sites since s172 (5 head-deref `GUARD` on `ctx->r4`, 5 walk-loop
`GUARD3` on `ctx->r3`), each written as `if (U32(ctx->rN) < 0x80000000u ||
U32(ctx->rN) >= 0x80800000u) goto <skip>;`. Neither guard fired this run.
Dispatched a research agent to read `recomp.h` (`N64Recomp/include/
recomp.h`, identical copy in this repo's `lib/N64ModernRuntime/N64Recomp/
include/recomp.h`) for the exact macro bodies:
- `U32(val)` = `(uint32_t)(val)` — plain truncation to the low 32 bits.
- `gpr` = `uint64_t` (`ctx->r4` etc. are 64-bit fields).
- `MEM_W(offset, reg)` = `*(int32_t*)(rdram + ((reg) + (offset) -
  0xFFFFFFFF80000000))` — uses the FULL 64-bit `reg`, no truncation.

Cross-referenced against the s99 lesson already in this doc (and
CURRENT-TRUTH ~line 343): a *correctly* sign-extended KSEG0 pointer has
upper 32 bits `0xFFFFFFFF` (that's why s99's guard, written to compare the
raw 64-bit `gpr` against a 32-bit literal, false-positived on 100% of calls
before being fixed to truncate through `U32()` first). This run's crashing
register (`x10=0x0000000080003827`) has upper bits `0x00000000`, not
`0xFFFFFFFF` — the same "KSEG0-zero-extension" shape already named for item
-49's `renderUnlitMeshFaces`/`0x80630062` bug and s210's
`evalCubicSplineAtTime`/`0x7ffffff8` bug (3 distinct exact values, so still
NOT one shared deterministic constant — but a 3rd independent function now
hit by the qualitatively identical corruption mechanism).

**The mechanism, stated precisely**: `U32()` discards the upper 32 bits
before the bounds check runs, but a legit sign-extended pointer
(upper=`0xFFFFFFFF`) and a corrupt zero-extended one (upper=`0x00000000`)
have IDENTICAL low-32-bit representations. Any guard using this exact
`U32(ctx->rN) < 0x80000000u || >= 0x80800000u` template is structurally
unable to tell them apart — not a coverage gap (missing site), a design
gap in the check itself. This template is used project-wide, not just in
heapWalker (same pattern at CURRENT-TRUTH doc lines ~3109/3402/3434/3622/
3777).

**Not yet done this session** (would require its own build+soak cycle,
against "one work unit" discipline): actually adding an upper-bits check
(`(ctx->rN >> 32) != 0xFFFFFFFFu`) to heapWalker's 10 existing sites and
soaking to see if the strengthened guard fires live for the first time.
That's the next work unit — see NEXT.md.

**Ruled out this session**: heapWalker's own existing GUARD/GUARD3 protecting
this run's crash site was not itself investigated for which of the 10 sites
is nearest pc+1128 — no disassembly tool is available (blocked, re-confirmed

uncovered 11th call. Irrelevant to the fix: the upper-bits check needs
adding to all 10 regardless.

## Session 215 (2026-07-28) — source-read reclassifies s214's do_send SIGBUS as
NOT the s176+ scheduler-UAF family; landed and soaked a new mesgqueue guard;
soak died to yet another unrelated pre-existing crash before the guard could
be exercised against the target, extending the "random unrelated crash wins
the race" pattern to a 6th consecutive session and surfacing a much higher-
value lead for next session

### Work unit: Option A from NEXT.md (chase the do_send SIGBUS)

Per NEXT.md's decision gate ("prefer A only if the source read in step 2
confirms same-mechanism quickly, within ~15 min"), read
`lib/N64ModernRuntime/ultramodern/src/mesgqueue.cpp`'s `do_send`/`do_recv`
and cross-referenced against the s176-184 thread-context-UAF mechanism
(`threads.cpp`'s `resume_thread_tagged`/`run_next_thread_and_wait`/
`wait_for_resumed`).

**Finding: the do_send SIGBUS is almost certainly NOT the s176+
scheduler-UAF family — it's a structurally different, more mundane bug.**
This build has no LTO (`grep -rn "INTERPROCEDURAL_OPTIMIZATION\|LTO"` on both
CMakeLists.txt files: 0 hits) and is `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` (confirmed via
`build/CMakeCache.txt`), so there is effectively no cross-translation-unit
inlining. `do_send` (mesgqueue.cpp) and `run_next_thread_and_wait`/
`wait_for_resumed`/`resume_thread_tagged` (threads.cpp) are separate TUs with
real out-of-line calls between them — a fault instruction inside any of the
threads.cpp functions would dladdr-symbolicate to THAT function's own symbol,
not to `do_send+388`. Since the crash's `[CRASH][pc-symbol]` line resolved
directly to `_Z7do_sendPhiibb+388` (established s213 as more precise than
`backtrace_symbols_fd`), the faulting instruction is almost certainly literal
code inside `do_send`'s own compiled body, not a callee.

The only unguarded native dereferences directly in `do_send`'s body are the
`TO_PTR(OSMesgQueue, mq_)` computation and the two
`TO_PTR(OSMesg, mq->msg)[...]` writes. `TO_PTR` (`ultra64.h:42`,
`#if 0`-gated native-compile branch confirmed dead, so the active branch is
always `((type*)(&rdram[(uint64_t)var - 0xFFFFFFFF80000000]))`) does
zero-bounds-checked pointer arithmetic on a raw 32-bit guest value — if `mq_`
(the guest `OSMesgQueue*` argument) or `mq->msg` (a struct field read out of
that same queue) is corrupted, the very next field access SIGBUSes with a
wild native address. This is the **same generic "unguarded TO_PTR on a
corrupted guest pointer" pattern already fixed at ~15 other sites this
project** (heapWalker's 10 GUARD/GUARD3 sites, `activateAnimationKeyframe`,
`composeNpcOrientationMatrix`, `rs_malloc`/`rs_free` call sites, the s78/s182
framebuffer refuse gates) — not a new investigation thread, and not the
scheduler-UAF mechanism s214 hedged toward ("this looks like the crash
variant of that same corrupted-thread-context family" — that framing is
**superseded** by this session's structural read; see CURRENT-TRUTH).

Also checked: `PTR(x)` is `int32_t` in the active build config (not the
64-bit-register case heapWalker's guards handle) — `mq_`/`mq->msg` are
already-truncated 32-bit values by the time C++ sees them, so this is a
simpler single-range bounds check, not an "upper 32 bits" check.

### Fix landed

`lib/N64ModernRuntime/ultramodern/src/mesgqueue.cpp`: added
`mesgqueue_guard_refuse(who, mq_)`, mirroring the s78
`FramebufferManager::get()` refuse-gate pattern — rejects (returns `false`
instead of dereferencing) any guest pointer outside `0x80000000`-`0x80800000`
(the same 8MB KSEG0/RDRAM bound used by every other guard site in this
project). Applied at the top of both `do_send` and `do_recv` (guarding
`mq_` before `TO_PTR(OSMesgQueue, mq_)`), and a second time on `mq->msg`
immediately before each `TO_PTR(OSMesg, mq->msg)` dereference in both
functions (4 call sites total) — `mq_` itself checked out doesn't guarantee
the struct's own `msg` field wasn't independently corrupted by the same
upstream heap-corruption family. Diagnostic: an always-on atomic counter
(`g_mesgqueue_guard_bad`) plus an `ROGUESQ_LOG_MESGQUEUE_GUARD`-gated
`fprintf` (always prints on the very first refusal regardless of the env var,
so a same-run positive control doesn't depend on remembering to set it).
Pure `lib/N64ModernRuntime` host C++, no guest regen needed. Built clean
(`cmake --build . -j8`, only pre-existing SDL2-version linker warnings).
Exported (`submodule-patches/export.sh`, refreshed
`submodule-patches/N64ModernRuntime.patch`, +100 lines) and committed this
session.

### Soak (`mesgqueueguard1`, copy of s214's `run_heapwalkerguard4.sh` env
block/`STICK_SCHEDULE`, `ROGUESQ_LOG_MESGQUEUE_GUARD=1` added)

Died at hold-iter 91 (~100s into the 300s hold) to signal 6 (abort):
`Assertion failed: (ctx->f2.fl == ctx->f2.fl), function mat3x3InverseInto,
file funcs_5.c, line 7582` — the project-wide `NAN_CHECK` safety assert
family (s83 `evalCubicSplineAtTime`, s214 soak 1 `sinfApprox`) firing at yet
**another** new call site. `[mesgqueue-guard]` fired **0** times,
`[heapwalker-guard]`/`[heapwalker-guard3]` (still armed, carried over from
s214's env block) fired **0** times, `[unlit-mesh-tracer]` **0** hits — the
process never reached the do_send/do_recv corruption window (if one even
exists on this run's random schedule) before dying to an unrelated crash.

**No direct positive control for "do_send/do_recv executed and passed the
guard cleanly N times" was instrumented** (the guard only logs on refusal,
not on every call) — a real gap, flagged for next session if this exact
question needs revisiting. Indirect evidence the guarded code path was live:
`[thr-resume] tag=run_next` fired part of 202,082 total `[thr-resume]`
events by the time of the crash, and `run_next_thread_and_wait` (which the
`tag=run_next` resumes trace back to) is reached **exclusively** through
`do_send`/`do_recv`'s blocking loops or `osStopThread`'s self-stop path —
so `do_send`/`do_recv` almost certainly ran many thousands of times this run
without the guard ever refusing, consistent with a genuine but rare
corruption event (s214 saw it exactly once) rather than dead/unreached code.

### Rules out / reframes

**Supersedes s214's "this looks like the crash variant of that [s176+
scheduler-UAF] family" framing** — this session's structural read (no LTO,
Debug build, dladdr resolves straight to `do_send`'s own symbol) makes it far
more likely the do_send SIGBUS is a plain corrupted-guest-pointer crash, the
same family as ~15 other already-guarded sites, not a new manifestation of
the multi-session scheduler stall investigation. Single-source (one
structural/source-level read, not cross-confirmed by a second independent
run) — flag as such if cited before a 2nd line of evidence lands (e.g. a
future soak where the guard actually fires with a wild `mq_`/`mq->msg`
value, or a future soak reaching the same SIGBUS with the guard still
silent, which would refute this session's read).

**Does not confirm or refute** whether the mesgqueue guard actually fixes
the target SIGBUS — the soak never got the opportunity. Neither confirmed
nor refuted, same "instrument armed but crash race lost to an unrelated bug"
outcome as s209/s210/s211/s214.

### The bigger pattern, and this session's real finding

This is the **6th consecutive session** (s209, s210, s211, s213, s214, s215)
where a soak of this general recipe family dies to a genuinely different,
previously-uncatalogued-at-that-call-site crash before reaching its intended
target — 3 of those 6 were `NAN_CHECK` assert firings alone (s83 lineage,
now at `evalCubicSplineAtTime`, `sinfApprox`, `mat3x3InverseInto` — 3
distinct call sites of the identical assert). Continuing to design ever-more-
targeted single-purpose guards one soak at a time, when a random *different*
pre-existing bug has better than even odds of winning the race first, is
hitting diminishing returns — each session characterizes and fixes one real

### Boring-thing-first check (step 1 of NEXT.md's plan) found a real gap

Before touching anything, verified which `recomp.h` the build actually
compiles against, per rule 5. **NEXT.md's premise was wrong**: it pointed at
`/Users/williambuckley/Documents/Tools/N64Recomp/include/recomp.h` (the
separate sibling checkout) and reasoned edits there wouldn't need
`export.sh` because that checkout isn't under this repo's `lib/`. But
`CMakeLists.txt:96/157/268` (`target_include_directories`) only ever adds
`${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/lib/N64ModernRuntime/N64Recomp/include` — a **second,
nested copy of N64Recomp that lives inside the `lib/N64ModernRuntime`
submodule as its own nested submodule** (`lib/N64ModernRuntime/.gitmodules`
has `[submodule "N64Recomp"] path = N64Recomp`). `RECOMP_FUNCS_DIR`
(`CMakeLists.txt:64`, `${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/../N64Recomp/RecompiledFuncs`)
does pull generated `.c` files from the sibling checkout, but their
`#include` of `recomp.h` resolves through the include path to the **nested**
copy, not the sibling one. The two files were byte-identical
(`diff` = no output) before this session's edit, which is why nobody had
been burned by this yet — but the nested copy is the one that's live, and it
**is** under this repo's `lib/`, so the "any edit under lib/ needs
export.sh + commit" hard rule applies to it.

Checked coverage: `submodule-patches/export.sh`/`apply.sh` only handled
`lib/N64ModernRuntime`, `lib/rt64`, and rt64's two nested contrib submodules
— **zero coverage for `lib/N64ModernRuntime/N64Recomp`**. Any prior or
future edit to files under that nested submodule (recomp.h or otherwise)
would have been silently unprotected: invisible to `export.sh`, lost on any
reset of the parent submodule, no patch to restore it from. Fixed this
session: added a `N64Recomp-nested.patch` export/apply pair to both scripts
(`submodule-patches/export.sh`, `submodule-patches/apply.sh`). Also had to
add `--ignore-submodules=dirty` to the `N64ModernRuntime` diff line —
without it, a dirty nested `N64Recomp` leaks a spurious
`Subproject commit ...-dirty` pointer line into `N64ModernRuntime.patch`
that `git apply` can't consume (caught this live: `N64ModernRuntime.patch`
grew from 958 to 964 lines on first export, traced to exactly this, fixed
before it was committed).

This gap-fix is a durable, standalone improvement independent of the
NAN_CHECK experiment's outcome — kept regardless of what the soak showed.

### Correcting NEXT.md's own line-range estimate

NEXT.md inherited an estimate that `heapWalker` was `funcs_3.c:99-7978`
(~7880 lines) and told this session to delegate the read to a subagent given
the size. Before delegating, checked it directly: `grep -n "^RECOMP_FUNC"
funcs_3.c` shows the *next* function (`countDisplayListChunks`) starts at
line 701 — `heapWalker` is actually **99-700, ~600 lines**. Small enough to
read directly in one `Read` call; no delegation needed. (The 7978 figure
seems to have been carried forward from an unrelated function's size at some
earlier session and never re-checked — exactly the kind of unverified
line-range NEXT.md's own instructions warned this session to confirm before
trusting.)

### Source read: the actual mechanism GUARD3 misses

Read the full function directly. All 5 per-mode-table sections share an
identical shape: load a table-sourced head pointer `a0`; if non-null,
dereference it once (`v0 = *a0`, the GUARD2/head-deref site, s157); if that
dereference is non-zero (list has 2+ entries), walk a loop:

```
v1 = a0;
LOOP:
    v1 = *v1;      // (A) GUARD3 (s172) validates the OLD v1 before this load
    v0 = *v1;      // (B) peek: dereferences the NEW v1 -- the value (A) JUST
                    //     read from heap/RDRAM memory, i.e. untrusted content
                    //     -- with ZERO validation
    if (v0 != 0) goto LOOP;
```
GUARD3 validates the pointer used to *produce* line (A)'s result, but never
validates the *value* that produces — and that value is immediately
re-dereferenced by line (B), one full iteration before GUARD3 would ever
re-check it (on the next loop-back, if the peek says "keep going"). This
structurally explains why the existing 10-site guard (`heapwalker-guard`/
`heapwalker-guard3`) has now stayed armed-and-silent (0/0) across **4
consecutive soaks** (s214 x2, s217, and every prior heapWalker-attributed
death) while the crash signature keeps recurring: GUARD3 was never
positioned to catch the deref that actually faults. Confirmed line (B)'s
`MEM_W(ctx->r3, 0X0)` call shape is byte-identical to line (A)'s, which
explains why both would produce the identical crash-address arithmetic
(`si_addr = corrupt_value + rdram_base`) when either one is the fault site.

Verified all 5 loops share this shape by direct read (not sampling one and
assuming): loop-back labels `L_80007A1C`/`L_80007A78`/`L_80007AD4`/
`L_80007B30`/`L_80007B8C` (matching `_heapwalker_guard3_sites` in
`fixup_game_funcs.py` exactly, confirming s172's list is complete for what it
guards), each followed immediately by the unguarded peek load at `+4`
(`0x80007A20`/`0x80007A7C`/`0x80007AD8`/`0x80007B34`/`0x80007B90`).

Also had to work out a safe bail target, which is *not* simply "the loop's
own postloop-append label" (e.g. `L_80007A2C`) the way GUARD3's bail target
is — that label's code unconditionally **writes through** the walked-to
pointer (`MEM_W(0X0, ctx->r3) = ...`, linking the list's tail into another
structure) before falling into the next block, so jumping there with a still-
corrupt `v1` would just relocate the fault a few lines later. Read forward to
find the first label that only touches `a0` (`ctx->r4`, the table-sourced,
structurally-trusted head pointer) and not `v1` — that's consistently 0x14
bytes past the postloop-append label in all 5 cases (`L_80007A40`/
`L_80007A9C`/`L_80007AF8`/`L_80007B54`/`L_80007BB0`) — and used that as the

CURRENT-TRUTH's housekeeping note on this file's persistence, unchanged this
session).

(`heapwalker-guard`/`-guard3`/`-guard4`/`heaplistdeq-guard`/`mesgqueue-guard`
all 0; `unlit-mesh-tracer`'s positive control fired once, confirming the
instrument itself works, but none of its labeled OOB-address sites fired).

Crash: signal 10 (SIGBUS), `[CRASH][pc-symbol] pc=... sym=renderUnlitMeshFaces
+792` (backtrace frame reads `+640` — the usual dladdr-vs-backtrace precision
gap, s213; dladdr is the trusted one). Backtrace:
`traverseSceneGraphRecursive` -> `processSceneNode` -> `renderUnlitMeshFaces`,
via `setupCameraMatrices` -> `static_5_800C9BF0` -> `menuOverlayInit` ->
`mainGameLoop` — **scene-graph rendering, not heap-walking at all**, the
first time this crash-literal has appeared outside the heap free-list-walk
family. Register dump: `x8=0x0000000300000000`, `x9=0x0000000080630062`,

instrument (which logs OOB `MEM_W` addresses at specific labeled sites in
this same function but didn't fire — this fault is at an untraced site
within it).

**Conclusion, three-source confirmed**: this is not a per-consumer bug that
per-site guarding will ever fully whack down — the identical corrupt 64-bit
literal (integer `3` in the upper 32 bits) has now surfaced in the heap
free-list-walker, the heap mode-table walker, and scene-graph mesh rendering,
three subsystems with no structural relationship to each other except that
they all eventually dereference *some* pointer-sized value. This is strong
evidence of a single shared corruption source (something writes this exact
bit pattern into a location many unrelated consumers later read), not
independent local bugs. **Recommended pivot for next session**: stop adding
consumer-side guards one call site at a time and instead hunt for the WRITE
site(s) capable of producing this literal — grep for anywhere a small
integer (a mode/generation/type tag equal to `3`) could get OR'd, shifted, or
raw-written into a 64-bit slot's upper half outside the `S32()`/`ADD32()`/
`U32()` discipline, and consider whether `ultramodern`'s native thread-
context save/restore (C++, not guest MIPS) could alias a stray `int` value
into a `ctx->rN`-shaped slot shared across these unrelated call sites. Full
detail above; soak artifacts: `scratch/s73_post_a_scene/heapwalkerguard4_1/`
(run.log), driver script
`scratch/s73_post_a_scene/run_heapwalkerguard4_1.sh`.

## Session 219 (2026-07-28) — refutes NEXT.md's "hunt the write site of the
literal `0x0000000300000000`" premise: that value is not corrupted data, it
is this process's constant native RDRAM host base pointer, already named as
such by s194 and never connected back to by s216-218; one of the "three
independent sightings" (s218's `renderUnlitMeshFaces` crash) is actually the
4th recurrence of a bug s194/s199 already diagnosed and precisely localized
20+ sessions ago and simply never fixed. Sourced-read that exact function,
found and shipped a guard for the one unguarded "peek-load on a freshly-read
list-walk pointer" site in it (same idiom as heapWalker GUARD4/
heapFreeListDequeue's guard), regenerated clean, and soaked to a **first**:
the full 300s hold window completed with **zero crashes** — but the new
guard's positive control (the pre-existing `unlit-mesh-tracer` call counter)
fired **zero times**, meaning `renderUnlitMeshFaces` was never even called
this run. Per rule 1, the clean soak is an uncontrolled null on this specific
fix, not a confirmation.

### Step 1 (NEXT.md): tabulating the three sightings turned up a fact NEXT.md's
own authors didn't have

Before writing any new instrumentation, did NEXT.md's own prescribed Step 1
(`grep -n "0x0000000300000000" PORTING-STATE.md`, build a table of session /
register / low-32-bits). The grep surfaced hits going back further than
s216-218 — to **s194** (`PORTING-STATE.md:17930-17968`) and **s199**
(`:19144-19211`), sessions the s216-218 lineage never cited. Reading those in
full changes the picture completely:

- **s194** (crash log still on disk,
  `scratch/s73_post_a_scene/mcontext1/run.log:4468133-4468166`): first-ever
  register-level crash dump, decomposed `si_addr` directly as `x0/x8
  (0x0000000300000000) + x9 (0x0000000080630062)` and stated explicitly:
  "`x0 =0x0000000300000000 (== x8; almost certainly the rdram host base
  pointer)`". s194 then derived the actual mechanism from `recomp.h`'s real
  `MEM_W` macro (`rdram + ((reg+offset) - 0xFFFFFFFF80000000)`, which only
  produces a valid ~8MB rdram offset because `ADD32` sign-extends a 32-bit
  guest value to `0xFFFFFFFF80xxxxxx` first): whatever computed this
  particular fault address added the RAW, zero-extended 32-bit guest pointer
  (`x9=0x80630062`, KSEG0 tag `0x8` intact, upper 32 bits zero, not
  `0xFFFFFFFF`) directly to the rdram host base with **no KSEG0 subtraction
  at all** — a different, unsafe code path from `MEM_W`. `lr` pointed at
  `processSceneNode+8772`, calling into an unresolved leaf.
- **s199** (log still on disk,
  `scratch/s73_post_a_scene/pcsymbolize1/run.log:4463555-4463585`): added a
  `dladdr`-on-raw-`pc` diagnostic (`[CRASH][pc-symbol]`, still permanent
  today) specifically to pin down that unresolved leaf, and got
  `sym=renderUnlitMeshFaces+508`, **byte-identical** `x9=0x0000000080630062`
  to s194 — confirmed same bug, 2nd occurrence, `decisionN` in the same
  9660-9800 band both times. CURRENT-TRUTH item -48 (superseded) and the s199
  entry both flag `renderUnlitMeshFaces+508` as "the single, precisely-scoped
  next work unit" — this was never picked up.
- **s216** (`heapFreeListDequeue`, raw dump: `si_addr=0x338d47580`,
  `x8=0x300000000` — the s216 writeup's transcribed `x9=0x0000000300000000`
  does not arithmetically reproduce its own stated `si_addr` and appears to
  be a copy-paste slip; the raw log for that specific run was not re-checked
  this session, budget permitting a future session should verify it
  directly).
- **s217** (`heapWalker`, raw dump re-pulled this session from
  `scratch/s73_post_a_scene/heaplistdeq1/run.log:140456-140491`, still on
  disk): `x0=x8=0x0000000300000000`, **`x9=0x0000000038d47580`** (not
  `0x80xxxxxx`-shaped — no KSEG0 tag), `si_addr=0x338d47580`, exactly `x0+x9`.
  This is a **different** low-32-bit value from s194/s199/s218's
  `0x80630062` and does not carry the KSEG0-tag shape at all — a separate
  bug from the renderUnlitMeshFaces one, not the same value recurring.
- **s218** (raw dump re-pulled this session from
  `scratch/s73_post_a_scene/heapwalkerguard4_1/run.log:169337-169370`, still
  on disk): `x8=0x0000000300000000`, **`x9=0x0000000080630062`**,
  `si_addr=0x380630062`, `sym=renderUnlitMeshFaces+792`. **Byte-identical
  `x9` to s194 and s199** — this is the SAME already-diagnosed bug's 4th
  recurrence (offset `+792` vs. `+508`, ~70 ARM64 instructions apart in a
  `-O0`/no-LTO build — plausibly two different call/loop iterations hitting
  the same faulting instruction, or a slightly different codegen offset from
  intervening unrelated patches over 20 sessions; not investigated further
  this session), not a new, independent "third sighting."

**Discriminating conclusion**: `x0`/`x8 = 0x0000000300000000` is a
**process-wide constant** (the host virtual address this build's mmap/malloc
happened to place the RDRAM buffer at — identical across every run for
months of sessions, which is itself consistent with a deterministic
allocator/ASLR-disabled layout, not evidence of a shared write). It appears
in every one of these dumps for the boring reason that `MEM_W` (and any
code imitating it) always adds rdram-base to compute a host address — of
course it's present whenever ANY memory access faults. **NEXT.md's premise
("hunt for the write site of this literal") has no target: there is no
write, and the "three-source-confirmed" framing in CURRENT-TRUTH item -59
conflates one already-solved bug (s194/s199/s218, 3 of the 4 same-value
sightings) with at least one structurally distinct one (s217, different low
bits, no KSEG0 tag) that happens to share the same uninteresting rdram-base
addend.** The real, per-site question was always "what corrupts/leaves
unmasked the OTHER operand (`x9`)" — precisely the question s216's and
s217's own source-reads already answered correctly for their own functions
(class A, upstream-corrupted-value propagation) without needing to invoke a
shared literal at all.

### Fix: renderUnlitMeshFaces list-walk peek-load guard

Read `renderUnlitMeshFaces` end to end
(`N64Recomp/RecompiledFuncs/funcs_4.c:4963-5630`, ~668 lines, no delegation
needed) specifically hunting for the same "peek-load on a freshly-read,
unvalidated list-walk pointer" gap GUARD4 (s218) fixed in `heapWalker` and
the loop-back guard (s217) fixed in `heapFreeListDequeue`. Grepped every
`MEM_W(ctx->rN, ...)` in the function for one immediately re-reading the
same register at offset 0 right after an assignment to it (the exact GUARD4
shape) — found exactly **one** such site, at `0x80011CE0`:

```
L_80011CDC:
    ctx->r18 = MEM_W(ctx->r18, 0X0);   // 0x80011CDC: validated by the
                                        // loop's own beq/bne structure
    ctx->r2  = MEM_W(ctx->r18, 0X0);   // 0x80011CE0: peek-load on the BRAND
                                        // NEW r18 -- zero validation
    if (ctx->r2 != 0) goto L_80011CDC;
```

No other `MEM_W(ctx->rN, offset)` pair in this function repeats the same
register at the same offset back-to-back — unlike `heapWalker`'s 5 identical
copies, this function has only the one. (This function also has 3 *other*
pre-existing, unrelated single-deref list-walk-shaped loads already covered
by the s208/s209 `unlit-mesh-tracer` observer sites A-D — none of those is
the double-deref shape; confirmed by direct inspection, not assumed.)

Shipped a guard (`fixup_game_funcs.py`, mirroring the `heapwalker_guard4`
template exactly: upper-32-bit check `r18_hi != 0xFFFFFFFF` — a bare
`U32()` truncated compare would silently PASS this corruption shape, per
s213's documented trap). Bail target: force `ctx->r18 = 0` then `goto
L_80011CEC` — that label is this loop's own natural exit, and it already
contains the exact "list is empty" handling
(`if (ctx->r18 == 0) { ctx->r10 = 0 | 0xFFFF; goto L_800120A4; }`) the
function was compiled with; forcing `r18=0` makes that pre-existing branch
fire correctly with no new semantics invented, the same "reuse the
function's own degrade contract" approach every prior guard in this family
uses.

Regenerated in the mandated order (`make_elf.py` → `N64Recomp` →
`fixup_game_funcs.py` → `cmake --build`). Fixup report confirmed the new
patch matched **exactly once** (`funcs_4.c: renderUnlitMeshFaces list-walk
peek-load guard (0x80011CE0) patched x1`), alongside the pre-existing
`heapWalker`/tracer patches re-applying normally (no double-apply, single
fixup run). Build clean (only the pre-existing `DDIV` pointer-sign
deprecation warnings, nothing new).

`fixup_game_funcs.py` lives in the untracked sibling `N64Recomp` checkout
(known, flagged risk since s83 — not this session's problem to fix); the
edit is on disk but outside this repo's commit scope, same as every prior
session's edits there. No `lib/` files touched this session — nothing to
export.

## Session 221 (2026-07-28) — found and closed the actual gap behind s220's `emitAllocatedDLCommand` hold-iter-1 crash: a 15+-session-old guard mechanism (s133) that only covered 2 of the function's 3 identical unguarded copies, not a new bug

NEXT.md's planned unit: source-read `emitAllocatedDLCommand`
(`funcs_3.c:2622-3210`, confirmed via `grep -n "^RECOMP_FUNC"` — matches
s220's estimate exactly) end to end and guard whatever unguarded
peek-load idiom explains s220's hold-iter-1 crash there.

**The read found something better than a new guard: the function already
has a guard mechanism for exactly this idiom, and it has a documented gap.**
Session s133 (PORTING-STATE.md:11791+) found that `emitAllocatedDLCommand`
inlines the same `findAndUnlinkSmallestEntry`-return-then-walk-to-tail-of-
chain idiom `submitSceneNodeRender` was guarded for (s123/s131), and shipped
`GUARD2` (validates the pointer before its first deref) + `GUARD3`
(validates the loop-back pointer inside the walk loop) via a generic
`_emit_dl_guard2_sites`/`_emit_dl_guard3_sites` table mechanism in
`fixup_game_funcs.py`. s133's own comment says the idiom is inlined "TWICE"
(an `r4` copy, an `r5` copy) and lists exactly two site-tuples per table.

**That count is wrong.** The idiom is inlined **three** times: `r4` is
reused by two *separate* copies (`findAndUnlinkSmallestEntry` call sites at
`0x800086C8` and `0x800087C4`), not one, plus the `r5` copy
(`0x800088C8`). s133 patched the *second* `r4` copy
(`0x800087D8`/`0x800087E4`, skip-label `L_80008814`) and the `r5` copy
(`0x800088DC`/`0x800088E8`, skip-label `L_80008918`) — but never the
**first** copy (`0x800086DC`/`0x800086E8`, skip-label `L_80008718`), which
is exactly s220's crash: s133's own original bug report backtrace
(`emitAllocatedDLCommand <- submitSceneNodeRender <- processSceneNode <-
traverseSceneGraphRecursive x2 <- setupCameraMatrices <-
runHangarSelectionFrame <- runHangarMenuFromOverlay <- menuOverlayInit`,
PORTING-STATE.md:11791+) is structurally identical to s220's. Confirmed by
direct source read (not grep-only): lines 2683-2703 have the raw
`MEM_W(ctx->r4, 0X0)` / `MEM_W(ctx->r3, 0X0)` pair with **no** guard block,
while the byte-identical-shaped code at 2862-2909 and 3063-3109 already
carries s133's guard blocks verbatim.

**This also explains a 15+-session-standing mystery, not just s220's
crash**: `emit-dl-guard2`/`emit-dl-guard3` have fired **0/0 in every single
soak since s133 shipped them** (s135, s139, s143, s148, s... — see
PORTING-STATE.md grep hits at lines 11876, 11942, 13044, 13084/13101,
13489/13503, 14952, 19322 — all "0/0", spanning ~85 sessions of elapsed
project history) despite `emitAllocatedDLCommand` demonstrably executing
every run. The standing explanation was some flavor of "this code path
isn't exercised" — but the real explanation may simply be that the two
*guarded* copies aren't the ones the game reaches, while the *unguarded*
first copy is.

**Fix**: added the missing site as a third tuple to both
`_emit_dl_guard2_sites` and `_emit_dl_guard3_sites` in
`fixup_game_funcs.py` (sibling `N64Recomp` checkout) — same template, same
bail-to-the-copy's-own-existing-null-check-label discipline (`L_80008718`,
exactly matching how the other two sites reuse `L_80008814`/`L_80008918`).
No new guard mechanism invented; this is closing a 3-vs-2 counting gap in
an existing one.
